result.summary: I've escalated the case at high priority. Copper Finch sent two invoices for the 5 February visit that overlap. Invoice A (£138, diagnosis) is within what the landlord authorised. Invoice B (£372) charges for an actuator replacement that was never authorised and that the records suggest never happened. Meanwhile a household with a child still has intermittent heating. Neither invoice should be paid until the contractor says which one is current. I moved the ticket to the landlord-approval stage, recorded the key facts, updated the tenant with safety advice and a date to expect news, and placed a 2-day hold.
result.situation: Tenant with a child reports intermittent radiator heating; hot water still works. The landlord authorised diagnosis only, up to £180 including VAT. The diagnostic visit on 5 Feb found a fault in the heating valve actuator. The landlord has not decided on the £372 replacement estimate. On 10 Feb the contractor sent invoice A (£138) and invoice B (£372), both with a 5 Feb service date. B says the replacement was done, but the evidence says otherwise. The contractor can't say which invoice is current. The landlord was asked on 12 Feb how to proceed and hasn't replied.

escalation.reason: Overlapping invoices, one charging £372 for actuator work that was never authorised or evidenced, while a household with a child still has intermittent heating.
escalation.handover_summary: Invoice A £138 matches the diagnostic quote and is within the £180 authority. Invoice B £372 claims the actuator was replaced on 5 Feb. That contradicts the contractor's own 5 Feb update (no remedial work), her estimate sent later that day asking for authorisation, the 7 Feb parts check, and the tenant's account (no visit since 5 Feb). No payment is recorded and no bank-detail change was requested. The contractor can't say whether B replaces A. The landlord was asked how to proceed on 12 Feb and hasn't replied.
escalation.recommendation: Don't pay either invoice yet. Ask Copper Finch in writing to withdraw invoice B and confirm A (£138) as the only charge; then send A to the landlord for payment. Phone the landlord for a decision on the repair, and consider a second quote if Copper Finch can't provide clear documents.

judgement.why_this_decision: The rules say never to pay or forward an invoice that doesn't match what was approved. Invoice B (£372) is for work outside the diagnosis-only authority (events 005, 012) and the records don't support it (events 008, 009, 016, 019, 020, 022). A disputed invoice and a vulnerable household both call for a human. Invoice A on its own would match, but it overlaps with B and the contractor can't say whether B replaces it (event 022), so A is held too. The landlord was asked on 12 Feb (event 023), so I didn't message him again or open a duplicate approval request.

alternatives_considered.option: Send invoice A to the landlord for payment now
alternatives_considered.why_not: The contractor hasn't confirmed whether B replaces A or overlaps it; paying A now risks a double charge or a muddled settlement.

alternatives_considered.option: Request landlord approval for £372 via a call
alternatives_considered.why_not: The landlord was emailed the same question hours earlier (event 023) and asked questions the contractor still hasn't answered (event 012). A duplicate request would be premature, so I've recommended a phone chase to the human instead.

alternatives_considered.option: Treat as an emergency and dispatch a contractor
alternatives_considered.why_not: Heating is intermittent, not fully off, hot water works, and there is no leak, gas smell or warning. It's urgent for a vulnerable household, but it doesn't meet the emergency threshold for acting without approval.
A disputed invoice plus a vulnerable tenant needs agency judgement.
